label: Hypopigmented and depigmented macules
q: Is the pigment reduced or absent, and is the surface normal?
lead: Two bedside observations settle most of this. Under a Wood lamp, amelanotic vitiligo glows chalk-white with sharp margins, while hypomelanotic lesions merely appear paler. And scale means the stratum corneum is involved — scrape it. A hypopigmented patch with reduced sensation is leprosy until proven otherwise.

stop.l: Hypopigmented patch with reduced sensation to light touch, pinprick or temperature
stop.a: Leprosy. Examine and palpate the peripheral nerves for thickening, test sensation across the patch, and refer to a leprosy service. Notifiable in most jurisdictions, and nerve damage is preventable only if caught early.

stop.l: Depigmented patch with an enlarging nodule or ulcer within it
stop.a: Consider amelanotic melanoma or squamous cell carcinoma in depigmented skin. Biopsy.

stop.l: Sudden widespread depigmentation with fatigue, weight loss or hyperpigmented mucosae
stop.a: Screen for autoimmune polyendocrine disease — particularly Addison disease and autoimmune thyroid disease.

stop.l: Ash-leaf macules in an infant with seizures or developmental delay
stop.a: Tuberous sclerosis complex. Refer for genetic and neurologic assessment and cardiac and renal imaging.

stop.l: White atrophic anogenital patches with itch, fissuring or bleeding
stop.a: Lichen sclerosus. Treat with a potent topical steroid and follow up — there is a squamous cell carcinoma risk, and any persistent nodule or ulcer needs biopsy.

stop.l: A fixed white atrophic anogenital plaque that is eroded or non-healing
stop.a: Biopsy to exclude squamous cell carcinoma complicating lichen sclerosus. Anogenital lichen sclerosus needs long-term surveillance for malignant change.

stop.l: A depigmented halo around an asymmetric or irregularly pigmented central lesion, or any halo lesion arising after age 40
stop.a: Halo depigmentation occurs around melanoma and melanoma metastases as readily as around a benign nevus. Excise the central lesion for histology rather than observing it, and examine the whole skin surface for a primary.

dx.look: Numerous small (2 to 5 mm), sharply defined, porcelain-white macules on the sun-exposed shins and forearms of older adults; entirely benign, they increase in number with age and photoaging and do not coalesce.
fr: Small (2 to 5 mm) discrete white macules that do not coalesce
Sun-exposed shins and forearms
Older adults, increasing with age
Sharply defined and irregularly shaped
Asymptomatic and individually stable
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis by the small size, number and photodistribution; no work-up is needed. Reassure that it is a benign feature of photoaging, not vitiligo.
dx.dsc: Well-defined white macules with a faint amoeboid or petaloid border and retained perifollicular pigment; smaller and more numerous than vitiligo.
dx.hp: Epidermal atrophy with reduced numbers of hypoactive (DOPA-poor) melanocytes and decreased basal melanin.
dx.assoc: A benign marker of cumulative sun exposure and photoaging (not autoimmune); reassurance is usually all that is required.
dx.mgmt: Reassurance and photoprotection; if treatment is wanted, a topical calcineurin inhibitor, localized cryotherapy or fractional laser may partially repigment lesions.

dx.look: Porcelain-white, atrophic, wrinkled (cigarette-paper) plaques with follicular plugging, most often anogenital (vulva, glans) and intensely itchy; a figure-of-eight perianal and vulvar pattern is classic. Anogenital disease scars, causes architectural loss, and carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk.
fr: Porcelain-white atrophic wrinkled plaques
Anogenital predilection with intense itch
Purpura or ecchymosis within lesions, and architectural scarring
A figure-of-eight vulvar and perianal pattern
Follicular plugging on extragenital lesions
dx.cf: Biopsy atypical, fixed or non-responding areas - anogenital lichen sclerosus carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk and needs long-term surveillance; distinguish morphea and vitiligo by the textural and atrophic change.
dx.dsc: Structureless white or whitish-yellow areas with keratotic follicular plugs and few linear vessels, and loss of the normal pigment network.
dx.hp: Epidermal atrophy with basal vacuolar change, a broad zone of upper-dermal hyalinization of collagen, and a band-like lymphocytic infiltrate beneath it.
dx.assoc: Anogenital disease scars and carries a squamous cell carcinoma risk, so it needs long-term follow-up; there is an association with autoimmune disease, especially thyroid. Biopsy fixed or non-healing areas.
dx.mgmt: An ultrapotent topical corticosteroid (clobetasol) is first-line and reduces symptoms, scarring and cancer risk, with long-term maintenance and surveillance for malignant change, plus emollients and gentle care.

dx.look: Chalk-white, completely depigmented macules and patches with sharply defined, often scalloped or convex borders, and a normal surface with no scale or atrophy. Periorificial, acral, and over bony prominences. Koebnerizes. Leukotrichia within patches. Fluoresces brilliantly under Wood light.
fr: Completely depigmented — chalk or milk white, not merely pale
Sharp, often convex or scalloped borders
Normal surface texture, no scale
Periorificial, acral, and extensor distribution
White hairs within the patch
Accentuates markedly under Wood light
Personal or family autoimmune history
ag: Confined to sites of previous inflammation
dx.cf: Wood lamp examination confirms depigmentation. Check TSH and thyroid antibodies, and consider FBC, glucose and, where clinically indicated, an autoimmune screen.
dx.dsc: Under Wood lamp a sharply demarcated bright blue-white fluorescence; on dermoscopy a residual perifollicular pigment with an absent pigment network in a well-defined white patch.
dx.hp: Complete loss of epidermal melanocytes and melanin (confirmed on immunostains) with a sparse lymphocytic infiltrate at active margins.
dx.assoc: Autoimmune thyroid disease is the commonest association - screen every patient (TSH with antibodies); also type 1 diabetes, pernicious anemia, Addison disease and alopecia areata.
dx.mgmt: A topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor for limited disease; narrowband UVB (the preferred phototherapy) for widespread disease; photoprotection and camouflage.

dx.look: Numerous small, round to oval, coalescing macules on the upper trunk, shoulders, neck and upper arms, with a fine branny scale released by gentle scratching — the evoked scale sign. Hypopigmented in tanned or darker skin, salmon or fawn in pale skin. Yellow-green fluorescence in some.
fr: Fine branny scale evoked by scratching the surface
Upper trunk, shoulders, neck, upper arms
Numerous small confluent macules
Hot humid climate, sweating, occlusion
Recurs each summer
dx.cf: KOH shows the spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern of short hyphae and clustered yeast — a near-instant confirmation. Adhesive tape stripping is an easy alternative sampling method.
dx.dsc: Fine branny scale accentuated by scratching or stretching; under Wood lamp a yellow-green fluorescence, over hypo- or hyperpigmented truncal patches.
dx.hp: Short hyphae and clustered spores (a spaghetti-and-meatballs pattern) in the stratum corneum on KOH or PAS, with minimal inflammation.
dx.assoc: Malassezia overgrowth favored by heat, humidity, oily skin and immunosuppression; the pigment change lingers after cure and recurrence is common.
dx.mgmt: Topical antifungals (ketoconazole, selenium sulfide, zinc pyrithione) first-line; oral itraconazole or fluconazole for widespread or recurrent disease. Counsel that repigmentation is slow.

dx.look: Ill-defined, round to oval, hypopigmented patches with very fine surface scale on the cheeks, upper arms and trunk of children and adolescents, often with an atopic background. More noticeable after sun exposure because surrounding skin tans.
fr: Child or adolescent
Cheeks and lateral upper arms
Poorly defined, feathered margins
Very fine surface scale
Atopic background
More obvious in summer
dx.cf: Clinical. KOH to exclude tinea. Reassure — it resolves spontaneously, though repigmentation takes months. Emollient and sun protection are the management.
dx.dsc: Ill-defined hypopigmentation with fine scale and a faint reduced-pigment pattern, without the sharp border of vitiligo.
dx.hp: Mild spongiosis with reduced melanin and a normal or slightly reduced melanocyte number - a low-grade eczematous process.
dx.assoc: A minor criterion of atopic dermatitis, mostly on children faces; benign and self-limited. Reassure that it is not vitiligo.
dx.mgmt: Emollients, sun protection and a low-potency topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor for inflammation; repigmentation is gradual.

dx.look: Hypopigmented macules and patches whose shape and distribution exactly reproduce a preceding inflammatory dermatosis — psoriasis, eczema, pityriasis rosea, lichen sclerosus, discoid lupus, or a burn. Partial rather than complete pigment loss.
fr: Shape matches a previous rash the patient can describe
Partial rather than complete pigment loss
Resolving over months
History of a preceding dermatosis or procedure at that exact site
ag: No preceding inflammation at that site
Complete depigmentation with sharp convex borders
Progressive spread beyond the original area
dx.cf: History alone. Repigmentation occurs over months to years. Look for and treat any residual active dermatosis, and protect from sun so the contrast fades.
dx.dsc: A reduced-pigment area matching a prior inflammatory lesion; a retained (though diminished) pigment network distinguishes it from vitiligo.
dx.hp: Reduced epidermal melanin with preserved melanocytes, sometimes with dermal melanophages from the antecedent inflammation.
dx.assoc: Follows eczema, psoriasis, infection or trauma; the distribution mirrors the prior dermatosis, and treating that condition allows recovery.
dx.mgmt: Treat the underlying inflammation and protect from sun; repigmentation occurs slowly once inflammation settles.

dx.look: Indeterminate and tuberculoid forms present as one or few hypopigmented or erythematous macules and plaques with a dry, anhidrotic surface, reduced or absent sensation within the lesion, and loss of hair. Thickened palpable peripheral nerves. Endemic in parts of South and Southeast Asia, Africa and South America.
fr: Reduced sensation to light touch, pinprick or temperature within the lesion
Dry, anhidrotic, hairless surface
Thickened palpable peripheral nerves — ulnar, great auricular, common peroneal
Few, asymmetric, well-defined lesions
Residence in or origin from an endemic area
dx.cf: Test sensation formally across the lesion and compare with adjacent normal skin. Palpate the peripheral nerves. Slit-skin smear for acid-fast bacilli and skin biopsy including nerves. Refer to a leprosy service — the priority is preventing nerve damage.
dx.hp: Tuberculoid - epithelioid granulomas tracking dermal nerves with few or no bacilli; lepromatous - sheets of foamy macrophages laden with acid-fast bacilli (Fite stain).
dx.assoc: The hallmark is sensory loss (temperature and light touch first) within the patch and enlarged peripheral nerves; confirm with skin biopsy (Fite) or slit-skin smears and classify as pauci- or multibacillary.
dx.mgmt: WHO multidrug therapy - rifampin, dapsone, with clofazimine for multibacillary disease - for a duration set by classification; monitor for and treat reactions; report to public health.

dx.look: Persistent hypopigmented patches with fine scale, most often on the trunk and buttocks, in children and young adults with darker skin types. Present for years, unresponsive to treatment for the eczema or tinea it has been labeled as.
fr: Persistent for years despite treatment
Darker skin phototype, often a child or young adult
Fine scale with mild itch
Trunk and buttocks, sun-protected sites
Repeatedly treated as eczema, tinea or pityriasis alba without response
dx.cf: Biopsy with immunophenotyping and T cell receptor gene rearrangement. This diagnosis is regularly delayed for years because the differential is dominated by benign conditions.
dx.dsc: Hypopigmented patches with fine short linear vessels and subtle scale; asymmetric and persistent.
dx.hp: Epidermotropic atypical lymphocytes with Pautrier microabscesses within a hypopigmented patch; repeat biopsies may be needed.
dx.assoc: A form of mycosis fungoides seen in younger and darker-skinned patients, easily mistaken for vitiligo or pityriasis alba when it fails to clear; send T-cell receptor gene rearrangement.
dx.mgmt: Skin-directed therapy - phototherapy (NB-UVB), topical corticosteroids or nitrogen mustard; refer to a cutaneous-lymphoma service.

dx.look: Present from birth or early infancy: lance-ovate or ash-leaf shaped hypomelanotic macules, often several, on the trunk and limbs. Best seen under Wood light in fair skin. Accompanied over time by facial angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas, seizures and developmental delay.
fr: Present from birth or early infancy
Lance-ovate ash-leaf shape
Three or more macules
Seizures, developmental delay, or a family history
Other cutaneous stigmata: angiofibromas, shagreen patch, periungual fibromas
dx.cf: Wood lamp examination and a full skin survey. Refer for genetic testing and for neurologic, cardiac, renal and ophthalmic assessment — the skin sign is often the earliest clue to the syndrome.
dx.dsc: A well-defined hypopigmented (lance-ovate) macule accentuated by Wood lamp, with residual perifollicular pigment (unlike vitiligo).
dx.hp: Reduced melanin with a normal melanocyte number and smaller, poorly melanized melanosomes.
dx.assoc: An early sign of tuberous sclerosis - look for three or more macules, then facial angiofibromas, a shagreen patch and periungual fibromas; evaluate CNS, renal and cardiac involvement.
dx.mgmt: The macule itself needs no treatment; the priority is recognition and referral for genetic and multisystem evaluation of tuberous sclerosis.

dx.look: A solitary, stable, well-defined hypopigmented patch with a characteristically serrated or feathered border, present from birth or early infancy, growing only in proportion to the child. Does not fluoresce as brightly as vitiligo.
fr: Present from birth or early infancy
Solitary and stable, growing only with the child
Serrated or feathered margin
Hypopigmented, never completely depigmented
dx.cf: Clinical, with Wood lamp showing accentuation without the brilliant chalk-white of vitiligo. Reassure — it is stable and benign.
dx.dsc: A stable, well-defined hypopigmented patch with a serrated or feathered border and retained perifollicular pigment; non-progressive, unlike vitiligo.
dx.hp: Reduced melanin with a normal or slightly reduced melanocyte number and impaired melanosome transfer - a functional defect, not melanocyte loss.
dx.assoc: Congenital or early, often segmental or blaschkoid, and stable for life; the task is to separate it from vitiligo (progressive) and the ash-leaf macule of tuberous sclerosis.
dx.mgmt: Benign and stable - reassurance, photoprotection of the patch, and camouflage if desired; no active treatment is needed.

dx.look: Ill-defined, nummular, non-scaly hypopigmented macules that coalesce over the trunk, particularly the back and the skin either side of the midline, in young adults with darker phototypes in humid climates. It looks exactly like pityriasis versicolor except that there is no scale, the KOH is negative, and antifungals have already failed.
fr: Ill-defined coalescing hypopigmented macules on the trunk and back
No scale, even after scratching the surface
Young adult, more often female, phototype IV to VI
KOH negative and no response to repeated antifungals
Punctate red follicular fluorescence within the macules under Wood light
ag: Fine branny scale evoked by scratching
dx.cf: A clinical diagnosis reached by exclusion. Scrape for KOH, which is negative, and examine under a Wood lamp for punctate red follicular fluorescence within the macules. The history is almost always of repeated antifungal courses that changed nothing.
dx.dsc: A structureless, ill-defined reduction in pigment with no scale and a retained but diminished pigment network. Under Wood light, punctate red follicular fluorescence within the macules is the finding that separates it from pityriasis versicolor.
dx.hp: Reduced epidermal melanin with normal melanocyte numbers and smaller, aggregated melanosomes; no fungal elements on PAS and minimal inflammation.
dx.assoc: Attributed to Cutibacterium (Propionibacterium) acnes within follicles rather than to Malassezia. Benign but persistent and cosmetically distressing, and repeatedly mistreated as tinea versicolor for years.
dx.mgmt: Antimicrobial and light-based therapy - benzoyl peroxide with topical clindamycin, or narrowband UVB, or both together; an oral tetracycline for extensive disease. Repigmentation is slow and relapse after stopping is common, so counsel accordingly.
dx.pat: Trunk, either side of the midline

dx.look: A round, symmetric, sharply defined white halo a few millimeters wide encircling a small central pigmented nevus, usually on the back of a child or young adult, and often several at once. Over months to years the central nevus fades and disappears, leaving a round white macule that eventually repigments.
fr: A round white halo centered on a small pigmented nevus
Back or trunk of a child or young adult
Several lesions at the same time
Halo symmetric and of even width
The central nevus is small, regular and evenly pigmented
ag: An asymmetric halo around an irregular or multicolored central lesion
No central lesion has ever been present
dx.cf: Clinical, with dermoscopy of the central lesion. Only one thing matters: what sits in the middle. If the central lesion is asymmetric, irregularly pigmented or in an adult, excise it - the halo phenomenon occurs around melanoma and melanoma metastases as readily as around a benign nevus.
dx.dsc: A symmetric globular or homogeneous central nevus surrounded by a structureless white rim. Asymmetry, an atypical network, a blue-white veil or irregular vessels in the center means excision rather than observation.
dx.hp: A dense band-like lymphocytic infiltrate destroying the nevus cell nests, with loss of melanocytes and melanin in the surrounding halo - an immune-mediated regression.
dx.assoc: Prevalence around 1%. It may herald vitiligo, so examine the whole skin and ask about personal and family autoimmune disease. Multiple halo lesions appearing in an adult warrant a full skin examination for a primary melanoma.
dx.mgmt: No treatment for a typical halo nevus in a child - photograph, reassure and review. Excise the central lesion if it is atypical or if the person is an adult. Photoprotect the depigmented halo, which burns readily.

dx.look: Depigmented macules indistinguishable from vitiligo at the bedside, but beginning exactly where a phenolic or catechol compound repeatedly met the skin - rubber gloves and footwear, adhesives, germicidal cleaners, hair dye. Confetti-like satellite macules around the main patches are characteristic, and lesions can later appear at distant untouched sites.
fr: Depigmentation began at the exact site of repeated chemical contact
Occupational or product exposure to phenols or catechols
Confetti-like satellite macules around larger patches
Other exposed workers or household members affected
Slows or improves once the exposure stops
ag: No identifiable exposure after a careful history
Classic periorificial and acral vitiligo pattern from the outset
Merely pale rather than chalk white
dx.cf: The exposure history is the diagnosis - ask specifically about gloves, footwear, adhesives, germicidal cleaners, cosmetics and hair dye, and about affected co-workers. Wood lamp shows complete depigmentation identical to vitiligo, and biopsy shows the same melanocyte loss, so neither test separates them.
dx.dsc: Identical to vitiligo - a sharply demarcated white area with an absent pigment network and residual perifollicular pigment. The history, not the optics, makes the distinction.
dx.hp: Absence of epidermal melanocytes, as in vitiligo. The histology cannot distinguish the two, which is why the occupational history is the test.
dx.assoc: Caused by para-substituted phenols and catechols - monobenzyl ether of hydroquinone, para-tertiary butylphenol and related compounds - that are selectively toxic to melanocytes. It clusters in workplaces, so notify occupational health and ask about affected colleagues.
dx.mgmt: Identify and remove the culprit chemical; this is the only step that changes the course. Then treat as for vitiligo with a topical corticosteroid or calcineurin inhibitor and narrowband UVB, with photoprotection and camouflage. Repigmentation is often incomplete.

dx.look: A round or oval plaque that is better felt than seen: indurated and bound down, ivory-white and shiny in the center, with a violaceous or lilac ring at the advancing edge. Hair and sweating are lost within it. A superficial macular variant produces confluent shining ivory-white patches that look exactly like extragenital lichen sclerosus, and a linear variant tracks down a limb or the forehead (en coup de sabre).
fr: Induration - the plaque is firmer than surrounding skin and better felt than seen
Ivory-white shiny center with a lilac or violaceous ring at the edge
Loss of hair and sweating within the plaque
Trunk or limb, or a linear band down a limb or the forehead
Slowly progressive over months, with no Raynaud phenomenon
dx.cf: Palpate before you look - induration is the diagnosis, and it separates morphea from vitiligo and post-inflammatory change in seconds. Confirm with a deep incisional biopsy including subcutis. Check Borrelia serology where the organism is endemic, and assess joints, limb length and eyes in linear disease.
dx.dsc: White fibrotic structureless areas with linear branching vessels and a peripheral erythematous halo, with loss of follicular openings within the plaque.
dx.hp: A normal to atrophic epidermis over a thickened dermis of homogeneous eosinophilic collagen, with an inflammatory infiltrate at the dermal-subcutaneous junction early and progressive loss of adnexal structures. Distinct from lichen sclerosus, which shows a broad upper-dermal hyalinized zone beneath an atrophic epidermis.
dx.assoc: Unrelated to systemic sclerosis, and there is no Raynaud phenomenon. Linear and pansclerotic forms cause flexion contractures, limb asymmetry and, on the head, ocular and bony atrophy - refer these early. Morphea and lichen sclerosus coexist in the same person often enough to look for both.
dx.mgmt: Potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids with topical calcipotriol or tacrolimus for limited plaque disease; UVA-1 or narrowband UVB phototherapy for widespread disease; methotrexate with systemic corticosteroids for linear, deep or rapidly progressive disease, where preventing contracture matters more than the color.

dx.look: A pale, irregularly outlined patch, usually on the trunk and often with satellite macules, that is not hypopigmented at all - the melanin is normal and the pallor is permanent local vasoconstriction. Rubbing it produces no erythema while the surrounding skin flushes, and pressing a glass slide across the edge makes the border vanish.
fr: Rubbing reddens the surrounding skin but not the patch
The border disappears under diascopy with a glass slide
No accentuation at all under Wood light
Present from birth or early childhood and stable since
Trunk, irregular outline, often with satellite macules
ag: Brilliant chalk-white accentuation under Wood light
dx.cf: Two bedside maneuvers settle it and neither costs anything. Rub the patch and the adjacent skin together - the patch stays pale while the surroundings redden. Then press a glass slide across the border: the margin disappears, because the blanched surrounding skin now matches it. It does not enhance under Wood light.
dx.dsc: No pigmentary abnormality - the pigment network is intact and only the vascular blush is reduced, which is itself the discriminating observation against every other entry in this differential.
dx.hp: Entirely normal skin, with normal melanocytes and normal melanin. The defect is a localized hypersensitivity of blood vessels to catecholamines, and no biopsy will show it - so do not order one.
dx.assoc: Usually isolated and benign. Multiple nevi anemici are described as an early cutaneous marker of neurofibromatosis type 1, so examine for cafe-au-lait macules, axillary and inguinal freckling and Lisch nodules, particularly in a child.
dx.mgmt: No treatment is needed or effective, because the melanocytes are normal. Reassure, and offer camouflage if the appearance matters.

dx.look: Depigmentation present at birth and stable for life: a white forelock over a triangular depigmented patch on the central forehead, with symmetric depigmented patches on the central chest and abdomen and the mid-portions of the limbs, sparing the hands, feet and mid-back. Islands of normal or hyperpigmented macules sit within the white patches - a pattern vitiligo does not produce.
fr: Present at birth and unchanged since
White forelock with a triangular frontal depigmented patch
Ventral midline chest and abdomen with mid-limb patches
Hyperpigmented islands within the depigmented areas
Family history in an autosomal dominant pattern
Dorsal midline of the back spared
dx.cf: Clinical, from the congenital onset, the stable ventral distribution and the hyperpigmented islands within the white patches. The step that must not be skipped is hearing: sensorineural deafness with iris heterochromia and dystopia canthorum indicates Waardenburg syndrome rather than isolated piebaldism, and audiometry in every affected child is the point of making the diagnosis.
dx.dsc: A sharply demarcated amelanotic area with an absent pigment network, containing discrete islands of retained or increased pigment - a pattern that separates it from vitiligo.
dx.hp: Absence of melanocytes in the depigmented areas with normal or increased melanocytes in the hyperpigmented islands, from a KIT mutation impairing melanoblast migration.
dx.assoc: Autosomal dominant, from mutation in KIT or rarely SNAI2. The critical differential is Waardenburg syndrome - congenital sensorineural deafness, iris heterochromia and dystopia canthorum - so arrange audiometry and an eye examination.
dx.mgmt: Stable and not medically treatable; photoprotection and camouflage. Autologous melanocyte suspension or punch grafting can repigment selected patches, and works better here than in active vitiligo precisely because the disease does not progress.

ctx.s: Pigmentary contrast is far more visible and more distressing in darker skin

ctx.l: Hot, humid climate or heavy sweating
Personal or family autoimmune disease, especially thyroid
From or resident in a leprosy-endemic region
Preceding rash or injury at exactly that site
Present for more than 3 years without change or response
Occupational or repeated contact with rubber, adhesives, germicidal cleaners or hair dye
ctx.s: Phenolic and catechol compounds are selectively melanocytotoxic, Fitzpatrick 8e §13

ctx.l: Family history of the same white patches, present from birth

find.l: Completely depigmented — chalk white, not merely pale
find.s: Amelanosis versus hypomelanosis is the primary division, Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction

find.l: Brilliant accentuation under Wood light with sharp borders
find.s: Wood lamp localizes and grades pigment loss, Fitzpatrick 8e Introduction

find.l: Fine branny scale evoked by scratching the surface
find.s: Evoked scale sign of pityriasis versicolor, Fitzpatrick 8e §26

find.l: Reduced sensation within the lesion
find.s: Anesthesia within a hypopigmented patch is near-specific for leprosy, Fitzpatrick 8e §25

find.l: Thickened palpable peripheral nerves
Dry, anhidrotic, hairless surface within the patch
Numerous small confluent macules on the upper trunk and shoulders
Periorificial, acral or extensor distribution
White hairs within the patch (leukotrichia)
Ill-defined, feathered or serrated margins
Shape reproduces a previous rash at that exact site
Present from birth or early infancy
Three or more lance-ovate macules with seizures or delay
Persistent for years despite adequate treatment
Buttocks or other sun-protected distribution with fine scale
Numerous small (2 to 5 mm) discrete white macules on sun-exposed shins and forearms
Porcelain-white atrophic wrinkled anogenital plaques with intense itch
Rubbing the patch reddens the surrounding skin but not the patch itself
find.s: Nevus anemicus does not show erythema after rubbing, Fitzpatrick 8e §13

find.l: The border disappears when a glass slide is pressed across it
Coalescing non-scaly macules on the back with punctate red follicular fluorescence under Wood light
Repeated antifungal courses for presumed tinea versicolor with no response
Depigmentation began exactly where a chemical or product repeatedly touched the skin
find.s: Chemical leukoderma follows contact with phenolic compounds, Fitzpatrick 8e §13

find.l: Confetti-like small satellite macules scattered around the larger patches
White forelock with a triangular depigmented patch on the central forehead
Hyperpigmented islands within the depigmented patches, in a ventral midline distribution
A white ring centered on a small pigmented nevus
Several round white macules on the back, some with a residual central pigmented dot
The patch is indurated and bound down, firmer than surrounding skin on palpation
find.s: Induration is the discriminating sign of morphea, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

find.l: Ivory-white shiny plaque with a lilac or violaceous ring at the advancing edge
find.s: The lilac ring of morphea, Fitzpatrick 8e §14

test.l: Biopsy of a fixed, eroded or non-healing anogenital plaque
test.w: White atrophic anogenital plaques that are fixed, eroded, thickened or not responding to a potent topical steroid.
test.p: Confirms lichen sclerosus and, importantly, detects any squamous cell carcinoma or differentiated intraepithelial neoplasia complicating it.
test.n: A benign biopsy is reassuring but ongoing surveillance is still required - malignant change can arise later.
test.x: Biopsy any non-resolving or thickened area; do not attribute new erosions to the disease without excluding cancer.

test.w: Every hypopigmented lesion. It takes seconds in a darkened room and separates amelanosis from hypomelanosis — the primary branch point of this whole differential.
test.p: Brilliant chalk-white accentuation with sharp borders indicates complete melanin loss and supports vitiligo. Yellow-green fluorescence suggests pityriasis versicolor in some species.
test.n: Mere pallor without brilliant accentuation indicates reduced rather than absent melanin, which points to pityriasis alba, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, or leprosy.
test.x: Less discriminating in phototypes V and VI, where the contrast is harder to grade. It also identifies coral-red erythrasma and green fluorescence of Microsporum tinea capitis, so use it more widely than for pigment alone.

test.l: KOH preparation or adhesive tape strip
test.w: Any hypopigmented macule with even a trace of scale, particularly on the trunk.
test.p: Short curved hyphae with clustered spores — spaghetti and meatballs — confirms pityriasis versicolor. Treat, and tell the patient the pigment takes months to return after the fungus has gone.
test.n: A truly scale-free lesion is not pityriasis versicolor. Move to the Wood lamp and the sensory examination.
test.x: Warn the patient in advance that clearing the infection does not immediately restore the color. Otherwise they return convinced the treatment failed, and get treated again unnecessarily.

test.l: Sensory testing across the lesion, and nerve palpation
test.w: Every hypopigmented patch, in every patient with a plausible geographic history. It costs nothing but a wisp of cotton wool and it is the test that prevents permanent nerve damage.
test.p: Reduced light touch, pinprick or temperature sensation within the patch, or a thickened peripheral nerve, mandates referral to a leprosy service and slit-skin smear.
test.n: Normal sensation across the whole patch makes leprosy unlikely, though very early indeterminate lesions may retain sensation.
test.x: Test with the patient's eyes closed and compare with adjacent normal skin. Palpate the ulnar nerve at the elbow, the great auricular in the neck, and the common peroneal at the fibular head.

test.l: Skin biopsy with immunophenotyping and TCR gene rearrangement
test.w: Persistent hypopigmented scaly patches in a young patient with darker skin that have failed treatment for pityriasis alba, tinea or eczema over years.
test.p: An epidermotropic CD8-predominant infiltrate with a clonal rearrangement supports hypopigmented mycosis fungoides. It usually responds well to phototherapy, so making the diagnosis matters.
test.n: A single negative biopsy does not exclude it. Repeat over time from a different patch.
test.x: Stop topical steroids for 2–4 weeks before biopsy. This diagnosis is routinely delayed for years because every item in the differential is benign and nobody biopsies.

test.w: At diagnosis of vitiligo and periodically thereafter, particularly with any suggestive symptoms.
test.p: Autoimmune thyroid disease is the commonest association and is treatable. Positive antibodies with normal function warrant continued monitoring.
test.n: Normal thyroid function does not exclude later autoimmune disease. Repeat if symptoms develop.
test.x: Ask about fatigue, weight change, postural symptoms and mucosal hyperpigmentation. Vitiligo can be the first sign of autoimmune polyendocrine syndrome, and Addison disease is the dangerous member of that group.

test.w: Any pale patch that does not accentuate under Wood light, particularly a stable trunk patch in a child. It takes ten seconds and needs only a glass slide and a finger.
test.p: Rubbing that reddens the surrounding skin while the patch stays pale, and a border that vanishes under a pressed glass slide, confirms nevus anemicus. No further investigation and no treatment are required.
test.n: If the patch reddens with rubbing and its border persists under diascopy, the pallor is melanin-based - go back to the Wood lamp, the scale and the sensory examination.
test.x: This is regularly skipped and the person is treated for vitiligo for years. Also check for cafe-au-lait macules and axillary freckling: multiple nevi anemici can be an early marker of neurofibromatosis type 1.

test.l: Wood lamp for punctate red follicular fluorescence, with KOH of the same site
test.s: Andrews' Diseases of the Skin; calibrated estimate
test.w: Non-scaly hypopigmented macules on the trunk of a young adult, particularly after antifungal treatment has failed.
test.p: Punctate red follicular fluorescence within the macules, with a negative KOH, supports progressive macular hypomelanosis. Treat with benzoyl peroxide and clindamycin or narrowband UVB rather than with another antifungal.
test.n: Fluorescence is not always demonstrable, and its absence with a negative KOH still leaves progressive macular hypomelanosis on the table. A positive KOH sends you back to pityriasis versicolor.
test.x: Examine in a properly darkened room and let the eyes adapt; the follicular fluorescence is faint. The larger error is prescribing a fourth course of antifungal for a non-scaly eruption that has never had scale.

test.l: Occupational and product exposure history, with a workplace survey
test.w: Any depigmentation that started at a site of contact, that involves the hands, feet or a strap or glove distribution, or that occurs in someone working with rubber, adhesives, cleaning agents, photographic chemicals or hair dye.
test.p: A consistent contactant, a matching distribution, and other affected workers together make the case. Remove the exposure and notify occupational health - other people are being exposed to the same agent.
test.n: A negative history does not exclude it, since the exposure may be domestic or cosmetic. Repeat the history at the next visit with a list of specific products in hand.
test.x: There is no laboratory test and no histologic marker - Wood lamp and biopsy are identical to vitiligo. If the history is not taken, the diagnosis is never made, the exposure continues, and phototherapy is given against an ongoing melanocytotoxic insult.

test.l: Palpation for induration, with a deep incisional biopsy including subcutis
test.w: Any white patch that feels different from the skin around it, and any linear white band on a limb or the forehead. Palpate every hypopigmented lesion before deciding it is pigmentary.
test.p: A thickened dermis of homogeneous eosinophilic collagen with loss of adnexal structures confirms morphea. Treat, and in linear or deep disease escalate to methotrexate early, because contracture and limb asymmetry are what cause harm.
test.n: A superficial punch showing normal dermis does not exclude deep morphea. Take a deep incisional specimen that reaches fat, or the sclerotic zone is missed entirely.
test.x: Two things are commonly missed. The macular variant of morphea is clinically indistinguishable from extragenital lichen sclerosus and the two coexist, so sample and look for both. And a linear plaque on a child's forehead or limb is not a cosmetic problem - it is a rheumatology referral.

test.l: Dermoscopy of the pigmented lesion at the center of the halo
test.w: Every white ring with a pigmented lesion in it, and especially any in an adult or any where the halo is asymmetric.
test.p: A symmetric globular or homogeneous central nevus in a child supports a benign halo nevus - photograph and review rather than excise. An atypical network, blue-white veil, irregular vessels or asymmetry means excision.
test.n: A reassuring central pattern in an adult still warrants a low threshold for excision and a full skin examination, because halo depigmentation also surrounds melanoma and melanoma metastases.
test.x: The trap is looking at the halo and not at what is inside it. The halo is never the diagnosis; the central lesion is. Multiple new halo lesions in an adult should trigger a whole-body examination for a primary melanoma.

flag: Test sensation in every hypopigmented patch where leprosy is geographically plausible. It costs a wisp of cotton wool and it is the only step that prevents irreversible nerve damage.
